status_reason: The 0.1 g/L guarantee cannot be given, and one Raman probe for glucose, ethanol and biomass is not supported; the fluorescence level, concentration ranges and fiber jacket are unknown.
answer: A 0.1 g/L glucose accuracy cannot be guaranteed before a test on your broth, and the sources support Raman for glucose but not for ethanol and biomass together. Strong autofluorescence can mask Raman, so the first step is a laboratory comparison of NIR plus fluorescence against Raman alone on live broth, using independent reference analyses. The 80 m silica fiber can carry Raman excitation at 680 or 785 nm, but its jacket must be checked for fluorescence first.

inline.headline: Test NIR + fluorescence on live broth in the lab against Raman alone, before ordering an in-line probe
inline.probe: Separate, time-synchronised NIR and fluorescence fiber probes for the lab test; a combined same-spot probe only if the broth proves heterogeneous at the probe
inline.install: Lab test first; the in-line position (vessel or recirculation loop) is to be chosen with the client after the test
inline.fiber: Silica fiber (Vis-NIR 350-2400 nm); the existing 80 m fiber must be checked for jacket fluorescence
inline.test_against: Raman alone (the client's concept) on the same broth samples
inline.not_final_because: Raman background from the broth is unknown, the fiber jacket is unknown, the concentration ranges and accuracy target are not given, and no validation data exist for this broth.

problems.text: A guaranteed 0.1 g/L glucose accuracy cannot be promised before validation; the sources give no accuracy figure for this application, and the method choice must be tested.
Strong autofluorescence can mask Raman signals, so a single Raman probe may not see glucose in this broth until the background is measured.
The sources support Raman for glucose, NIR for glucose and glycerol, and UV-Vis for biomass; none shows one Raman probe measuring glucose, ethanol and biomass together.
Silica transmits the 680 and 785 nm Raman excitation, but a polymer jacket can add fluorescence; the jacket of the existing 80 m fiber is unknown, and the sources give no loss data for that length.

methods.why: Most common online fiber-probe method; tracks glucose in the millimolar range but may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %; ethanol bands at 1.5-2.2 µm lie within the silica range, while the 6-10.5 µm glucose and ethanol bands lie beyond the 2400 nm silica limit.

Detects intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin at high sensitivity; NIR plus fluorescence gave more accurate biomass in yeast fermentation and separated intra- and extracellular metabolites.
The client's concept; detects glucose directly in aqueous media, but strong fluorescence can mask it, so it serves as the comparison arm rather than the in-line choice.
Low-cost biomass signal from turbidity; UV-ATR suits turbid or concentrated media where transmission saturates, so it is useful only as a cheap biomass check.

questions.q: What concentration ranges and units do you expect for glucose, ethanol and biomass, and what accuracy would you need to validate against?
questions.why: NIR may lack sensitivity below 0.1 %, which is in different units from the 0.1 g/L target.

questions.q: Does the broth fluoresce strongly at the excitation you would use, and can you provide a spectrum of the broth with and without yeast?
questions.why: Fluorescence decides whether Raman is usable at all and sizes the fluorescence signal for any fused model.

questions.q: What is the jacket material of the existing 80 m fiber, and what loss did it measure at the wavelengths you would use?
questions.why: A polymer jacket can add fluorescence to Raman and fluorescence signals; the sources describe 100-300 m cables, not 80 m.

questions.q: Where in the process would the probe sit, and is the broth homogeneous at that point?
questions.why: Heterogeneous samples need both methods on the same spot; homogeneous broth allows separate synchronised probes.

experiment.objective: Decide whether NIR plus fluorescence beats NIR, fluorescence and Raman alone for glucose, ethanol and biomass on live broth, measured against independent laboratory analyses.
steps: Collect broth samples across the fermentation run, covering the client's concentration ranges, and measure glucose, ethanol and biomass by independent laboratory analyses as reference.
Record NIR, fluorescence and Raman spectra (Raman at 785 nm, and 680 nm if available) on the same synchronised samples, and note the fluorescence background at each excitation.

Build PLS models for each method and for the NIR plus fluorescence low-level fusion, using the same calibration and held-out validation samples; use segmented cross-validation and a randomisation test.
Pass light through a reel of the same fiber type, or the 80 m fiber if accessible, at the excitation and detection wavelengths, and record transmission and jacket fluorescence.
Compare the validation results; order hardware only if the fused model beats the best single method and meets the client's go/no-go criteria.
references: AFS S01 p.7 (NIR plus fluorescence, yeast fermentation)
AFS S01 p.14-15 (low-level fusion of synchronised spectra with PLS)
AFS S03 p.14 (segmented CV and randomisation tests)

pathway.key_features: NIR ethanol bands at 1.5-2.2 µm; fluorescence emission from intrinsic fluorophores such as NADH, tryptophan and riboflavin; Raman glucose signal above the fluorescence background, to be found in the lab.
pathway.path_reason: Key spectral features and a validated model must come from the lab test before a path is chosen.

multispectral.why: Complementary information: NIR gives broad overtone bands for bulk composition that need chemometrics, while fluorescence gives intrinsic fluorophore signals; this pair gave more accurate yeast biomass and separated intra- and extracellular metabolites.
multispectral.test: On the same synchronised lab samples, the same validation split and independent reference values, the fused NIR plus fluorescence model must beat the best single model (NIR, fluorescence or Raman); if not, use the best single method.
